--- Page 1 ---
Agent-written heuristics versus commercial solvers on unsolved
job-shop benchmark instances
Andre Albrecht1,*, Enzo Morosini Frazzon1, Leandro C. Coelho2 and Bruno Vieira1,3
1ProLogIS – Production and Logistics Intelligent Systems, Department of Production Engineering, Federal
University of Santa Catarina (UFSC), Florianópolis, SC, 88040-900, Brazil
2CIRRELT and Canada Research Chair in Integrated Logistics, Université Laval, Québec, QC, G1V 0A6, Canada
3Department of Industrial Engineering, Federal Institute of Santa Catarina (IFSC), Caçador, SC, 89503-550, Brazil
andre.albrecht@posgrad.ufsc.br, enzo.frazzon@ufsc.br, leandro.coelho@fsa.ulaval.ca,
bruno.vieira@ifsc.edu.br
*Corresponding author
Preprint submitted to International Transactions in Operational Research, November 2026
Abstract
Commercial solvers are the standard tool for difficult scheduling problems. We study whether a
frontier large language model, used as a coding agent with open-source tools only, can match them
in quality and speed. We report every run, and independent checkers verify every schedule. On
the 100,000-operation job shop tai_100_1000_1, an agent-written solver reached 525,515, below
OptalCP, Hexaly, and CP Optimizer. Unchanged, it improved all ten instances of the family and closed
two. With equal budgets on the same workstation, it ended 0.0–1.8% above the lower bound, against
2.6–5.8% for CP Optimizer and 2.4–4.4% for Hexaly. On the Behnke–Geiger flexible job shops, an
agent-written tabu search improved 11 of 32 open instances. With two transport robots, an agent-
written solver improved seven of ten MKT instances. New lower bounds show that four published
MKT values cannot be attained on the distributed instance files. Agent-run improvement campaigns
closed eight further instances.
Keywords: job shop scheduling; flexible job shop; transport robots; lower bounds; large language models;
coding agents; heuristic design; commercial solvers; benchmark
1
Introduction
Scheduling problems arise in manufacturing and logistics (Leusin et al., 2018), and many practitioners
solve them by means of commercial solvers. Typical examples are Hexaly (Hexaly, 2026a; Benoist et al.,
2011), IBM ILOG CP Optimizer (Laborie et al., 2018), Gurobi, and OptalCP (ScheduleOpt, 2026c).
These solvers perform very well on a wide range of problems and need little problem-specific work, but
commercial use requires a paid license. Hexaly and OptalCP quote their commercial prices on request
(Hexaly, 2026b; OptalCP, 2026b), and IBM lists a developer subscription of CP Optimizer from US$320
per user and month, with deployment licenses on request (IBM, 2026). These three are free for academic
use. Open-source solvers such as OR-Tools CP-SAT (Google, 2024; Perron et al., 2023) are free, but on
large scheduling instances they are often weaker (Da Col and Teppan, 2022; Yuraszeck et al., 2026).
At the same time, large language models (LLMs) can now write and run code in long autonomous
sessions (Chen et al., 2021; Jimenez et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024b). Recent work uses LLMs to design
heuristics (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024a; Ye et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025) and to
formulate optimization models (Ramamonjison et al., 2022; AhmadiTeshnizi et al., 2024; Huang et al.,
2025). Scheduling is a natural test for such agents, because a candidate schedule is easy to check, whereas
a good schedule is difficult to find.
1
arXiv:2611.17682v1  [math.OC]  13 Nov 2026


--- Page 2 ---
Our starting question is whether a frontier LLM, used as a coding agent, can replace an off-the-shelf
commercial solver. We aimed for results of similar quality in a similar time. The agent had no access to a
commercial solver, and it could use only open-source tools and the code it wrote itself.
The results exceed this target. The agents analyzed the structure of each instance and, when the standard
formulation did not yield good solutions, they changed it. They then wrote heuristics and metaheuristics
tailored to that structure, and used open-source tools such as CP-SAT for subproblems and bounds. On the
job shop and the flexible job shop, the results are better than the best published values of the commercial
solvers, and better than CP Optimizer and Hexaly in our own runs with the same budget on the same
workstation. For the transport problem, the results are better than all valid published values on seven of
the ten MKT instances, including the largest ones, better than the CP Optimizer models of Meng et al.
(2025) on nine of them, and better than CP-SAT with four times the CPU time. We do not count four
published values on these instances, because they are below a new lower bound on the distributed instance
files, nor two published schedules that assign an operation to a machine on which it is not eligible. On the
Chambers–Barnes transport instances, where processing times dominate travel times, the CP Optimizer
approach is better than the agent-written solver.
The contributions of the paper can be summarized as follows:
• We propose a method to test LLM coding agents on open benchmark instances, with a clear split
between autonomous runs and runs with human help (Section 5).
• We provide new best-known schedules for three established problem families: the 100 × 1000 job
shops of Da Col and Teppan (2022), the flexible job shops of Behnke and Geiger (2012), and the
flexible job shops with transport robots of Homayouni and Fontes (2021) (Section 6).
• We derive new lower bounds for the flexible job shop with transport robots and validate them with
two solvers. They are above eleven published values on the distributed instance files and certify
eight published schedules as optimal, two of them (MFJST09 and mt10xyzt) without a previous
proof (Sections 3.2 and 6.4).
• We compare the quality, speed, and cost of the agent-written solvers with those of commercial and
open-source solvers on the same instances (Sections 6 and 7), and three ways to use an agent: as
the solver itself, as the author of a reusable solver, or as the improver of such a solver in its own
campaign (Section 5.3).
• We test the agent-written solvers on similar instances without any change. On the job-shop family,
the solver has improved the best-known values of all ten instances and has solved two open instances
to optimality (Section 6.2).
We report every agent run on the instances of this paper, without any selection based on the results.
An independent checker verifies every schedule, and a public repository contains all instances, schedules,
checkers, solvers, solver logs, and task texts (see the statement on data availability).
The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we review the literature on shop
scheduling, on the flexible job shop with transport robots, and on LLMs for optimization. The three
problems and new lower bounds for the problem with transport robots are formally described in Section 3,
and their selection in Section 4. In Section 5 we present our experimental method, followed by extensive
computational experiments in Section 6 and a discussion in Section 7. Conclusions follow in Section 8,
and Appendix A lists all new best-known values.
2
Literature review
2.1
Solvers and benchmarks for shop scheduling
The job shop and the flexible job shop are classical NP-hard problems (Garey et al., 1976; Brandimarte,
1993), and methods are compared on public benchmark libraries (Taillard, 1993; Beasley, 1990). JSPLib
2


--- Page 3 ---
(ScheduleOpt, 2026b) and FJSPLib (ScheduleOpt, 2026a) record the best-known lower and upper bounds
of each instance, together with the solver and the hardware that produced them. JSPLib also publishes
a standard 10-minute comparison of CP Optimizer, CP-SAT, OptalCP, and CPLEX on every instance.
Naderi et al. (2023) and Yuraszeck et al. (2026) have compared constraint programming and mixed-integer
programming solvers on thousands of shop instances, and Da Col and Teppan (2022) have generated very
large Taillard-type job shops to test how CP Optimizer and CP-SAT scale. Good practice for computational
experiments requires public data, independent verification, and the reporting of all runs (Barr et al., 1995;
Hooker, 1995; Gleixner et al., 2021). We follow these rules in this paper.
2.2
Flexible job shops with transport robots
In many plants, automated guided vehicles (AGVs) move jobs between machines, so machines and vehicles
must be scheduled together (Bilge and Ulusoy, 1995; Hosseini et al., 2024). The same integration of
production and transport scheduling also arises along supply chains (Frazzon et al., 2018). Homayouni
and Fontes (2021) have proposed a standard benchmark for this problem, the flexible job shop with transport
(FJSPT). It adds a load/unload station, travel times, and two vehicles to the instances of Brandimarte (1993),
Chambers and Barnes (1996), and others. The small instances can now be solved exactly (Ham, 2020;
Homayouni and Fontes, 2021; Yao et al., 2025, 2026; Wang, 2025).
For the large instances, several
heuristic methods have published results: late-acceptance hill climbing (LAHC) (Homayouni and Fontes,
2021; Burke and Bykov, 2017), a biased random-key genetic algorithm (Homayouni et al., 2023), an
improved genetic algorithm (IGA) (Meng et al., 2023), a dual population genetic algorithm (DCGA) (Han
et al., 2024), a tabu search (Berterottière et al., 2024), a variable neighborhood descent genetic algorithm
(IVNDGA) (Jia et al., 2025), a deep reinforcement learning method (HA-DQN) (Dong et al., 2025), and
an ant colony hybrid (He et al., 2025). Meng et al. (2025) have proposed constraint programming models
and a metaheuristic assisted by these models for this benchmark, and Liu et al. (2026b) have compared a
learned policy with the best values of several of these methods. In this literature, the problem is also called
the FJSP-AGV.
2.3
LLMs for optimization and scheduling
LLMs support optimization in two main ways. In the first, the LLM writes a model that a standard
solver then solves, as in NL4Opt (Ramamonjison et al., 2022), OptiMUS (AhmadiTeshnizi et al., 2024),
Chain-of-Experts (Xiao et al., 2024), and ORLM (Huang et al., 2025). Alternatively, the LLM writes or
improves heuristics inside an evolutionary loop, as in FunSearch (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024), OPRO
(Yang et al., 2024a), EoH (Liu et al., 2024a), ReEvo (Ye et al., 2024), AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025),
and the LLM4AD platform (Liu et al., 2024b). Recent literature reviews can be found in Liu et al. (2026a)
and Da Ros et al. (2026).
In scheduling, LLMs have been used to generate schedules directly (Abgaryan et al., 2024, 2025), to
design operators and dispatching rules for the flexible job shop (Liao et al., 2025; Cao and Yuan, 2025), and
to coordinate multi-agent scheduling pipelines (Wang et al., 2025). Sánchez-Fernández et al. (2026) have
tested whether LLM agents can write correct constraint programming models for six industrial scheduling
problems. However, these studies mostly measure the correctness of models, or compare against simple
baselines on small instances.
Our study differs from these papers in three ways. First, the agent writes a complete solution method,
not only a model or a single operator. Second, the targets are large open instances with strong published
bounds, most of them from commercial solvers. Third, the agent works in a general coding environment,
without a special framework, an evolutionary loop, or task-specific training.
3


--- Page 4 ---
3
Problem description
3.1
Problem definitions
We now formally introduce the three problems studied in this paper. In the job shop scheduling problem, a
set J of n jobs must be processed on a set M of m machines. Each job j ∈J is a sequence of operations,
and operation o of job j requires machine µj,o for pj,o time units without preemption. The operations of
a job must follow this sequence, and a machine processes at most one operation at a time. The aim is
to determine the start time sj,o of each operation, so that all constraints are satisfied and the makespan
Cmax = maxj,o{sj,o +pj,o} is minimized. Let Lj = P
o pj,o be the length of job j. The value maxj∈J Lj
is a lower bound on Cmax.
The flexible job shop scheduling problem extends this problem with a choice of machine. Operation o
of job j can be processed on any machine k of a set Mj,o ⊆M, with a processing time pj,o,k. The aim is
to determine the machine and the start time of each operation, so that the makespan is minimized.
The FJSPT adds a load/unload station and a set V of identical vehicles to the flexible job shop
scheduling problem. Location 0 represents the station, and ta,b is the travel time from location a to location
b, with a, b ∈{0} ∪M. All jobs and all vehicles are at location 0 at time zero. Each operation requires a
loaded trip from the location of its predecessor to its machine, where location 0 is the predecessor of the
first operation of a job. No trip is required if two consecutive operations of a job use the same machine.
A trip departs after the completion of the preceding operation, and the operation starts after the arrival of
the trip. A vehicle carries one job at a time, travels empty from each drop-off to its next pickup, and may
wait. The buffers at the machines are unlimited, and the jobs do not return to location 0. The aim is to
determine the machine of each operation, the vehicle of each trip, and all start times, so that the makespan
is minimized. All instances of this paper have |V | = 2. The three problems are NP-hard since they contain
the job shop scheduling problem as a special case (Garey et al., 1976).
3.2
Lower bounds for the FJSPT
The best published lower bounds of the FJSPT (Homayouni and Fontes, 2021, Eqs. 26–27) are the longest
path of a job through processing and loaded travel, and the total shortest loaded travel shared among the
vehicles. They do not include empty travel. However, jobs never return to location 0, so the vehicles must
make at least n −|V | empty trips to this location. We now derive a lower bound based on this observation.
We charge each empty trip at the length of a shortest path between its end points. This is conservative,
because on the layouts that violate the triangle inequality, it is shorter than the direct travel time of the
benchmark. Let Wv be the total loaded and empty travel time of vehicle v in a schedule, and let qv be
the processing time of the operation that v delivers last plus the shortest remaining processing and loaded
travel time of its job. The last drop-off of v occurs no earlier than Wv, so Cmax ≥Wv + qv, and thus
|V ′| Cmax ≥P
v∈V ′(Wv + qv) for the set V ′ of vehicles used. In addition, let ℓk be the total processing
time assigned to machine k, and let hk and tk be the smallest earliest start and the smallest remaining time
after completion among the operations that are eligible on k, computed with the operation on k. If machine
k is used, then Cmax ≥hk + ℓk + tk. Finally, Cmax is at least the processing and loaded travel time along
the path of each job. We minimize Cmax subject to these inequalities over all machine assignments and
all vehicle routes, without any other timing constraint. This yields a small integer program, in which each
job is a path through its eligible machines, the empty trips balance the loaded trips at each location, and at
most |V | routes start at location 0. Its optimal value, rounded up to the time granularity of the instance, is
a lower bound on Cmax. We refer to it as bound (1).
The first of these inequalities yields a closed-form bound, bound (2), that requires no solver. Let πa be
the length of a shortest path from location a to location 0. An empty trip from a to b takes at least πa −πb
time units. If we sum these differences over all empty trips, the terms of the loaded trips telescope along
each job. Thus, the total empty time is at least P
j∈J πfj −P
v∈V πev, where fj is the last machine of
job j and ev is the location of the last drop-off of vehicle v. Let Aj be the minimum, over all machine
sequences of job j, of its loaded travel time plus πfj. Let τ be the minimum, over all machines k, of the
smallest processing time on k minus πk. Then Cmax ≥P
j∈J Aj/|V | + τ.
4


--- Page 5 ---
When processing times dominate travel times, a second relaxation is more useful. We remove the
capacity of the vehicles and the empty trips, and we keep each loaded trip as a delay between two
consecutive operations of a job. The result is a flexible job shop with travel delays, which we solve by
means of CP-SAT. Its optimal value is also a lower bound on Cmax, because every schedule of the FJSPT
is feasible for this relaxation. We refer to it as relaxation (3).
4
Problem selection
We selected problems that are established, have tracked bounds, are open, are large and complex, and are
checkable. They have been in the literature for several years with public instance files, a public table or a
recent paper gives their best-known bounds and the solver that found them, commercial solvers are often
far from the lower bound, and the feasibility of a schedule can be checked easily with independent code.
Table 1 lists the selected instances. The job shop tai_100_1000_1 has 100 jobs, 1,000 machines, and
100,000 operations (Da Col and Teppan, 2022). JSPLib lists it as open, with recent bounds from OptalCP,
CP Optimizer, and Hexaly (ScheduleOpt, 2026b; Yuraszeck et al., 2026). From the Behnke–Geiger flexible
job shops (Behnke and Geiger, 2012), we have selected the open instances behnke16 and behnke14, and
the closed instance behnke31 as a control, since a good method should find its known optimum. For the
flexible job shop with transport robots, we have used the benchmark of Homayouni and Fontes (2021),
the standard benchmark for this problem, on which several later methods report results (Meng et al.,
2023; Berterottière et al., 2024; Dong et al., 2025). The problem adds a second, interacting resource
(the vehicles) to the flexible job shop, which makes it a good representative of integrated production and
logistics scheduling (Frazzon et al., 2018). From this benchmark, we have selected the ten MKT instances
and the 21 Chambers–Barnes instances. They are the largest sets, and published heuristics were far from
the published lower bounds. However, Meng et al. (2025) report 14 of the 21 Chambers–Barnes instances
as solved to optimality with CP Optimizer (Section 6.4). The smaller sets are mostly solved to optimality,
so we have used them only to test generalization. In Table 1, LB and UB are the best-known lower and upper
bounds before this work. For the transport instances, LB is the best published lower bound (Homayouni
and Fontes, 2021). The asterisk marks the control instance.

5
Method
5.1
Framework and technology stack
Figure 1 shows the framework of our study. In autonomous runs, the task is the only input. In assisted runs,
we have also provided goals and papers, and we have managed the compute resources (dashed arrow).
An independent checker verifies every output schedule. The agent is Claude Code (Anthropic, 2026a), a
command-line coding agent. It reads files, writes code in any language, compiles and runs it, reads the
output, and repeats this loop until the time budget ends. Table 2 lists the models, the hardware, and the
software.

5.2
Autonomous runs and assisted runs
Our main goal is to verify whether the agent is able to obtain good solutions without expert knowledge.
We therefore distinguish two types of runs.
In an autonomous run, the agent was given one task: improve the makespan of one instance. The
task text described the instance format, the rules, the output format, and a target. For tai_100_1000_1,
the target was a makespan strictly below 540,000. For behnke16, the text asked for a heuristic, stated
the best-known upper bound of 412, and set the target 411. The agent then worked without human input
in a new container, with a fixed amount of time and of CPU cores, and it selected its own method. An
independent test checked the schedule at the end. One job-shop session also received code written by an
earlier session and the best value then known.
In an assisted run, we worked with the agent in an interactive session on the workstation. We gave
goals and feedback, supplied papers, and managed the compute resources (for example, how many cores a
solver could use), but we did not write any solver code. Table 3 shows the type of each run.
5.3
Modes of use of the agent
We have tested three modes of use. In mode A, the agent itself is the algorithm, and it must deliver a
good schedule for one instance. It may write code that is used only once, and it does not have to leave a
reusable program. If a new schedule is needed, the agent is run again. In mode B, the agent must deliver
a solver that the user can compile and run again, on the same instance or on similar ones. The cost then
6


--- Page 7 ---
shifts from LLM tokens to CPU time. In mode C, the agent starts from the outcome of modes A and
B, namely the solvers and best schedules of this paper, and runs its own improvement campaign with the
goal of closing as many instances as possible. It may change the solvers, write new code, and select the
experiments to run. We have run mode C once on the job shop and once on the flexible job shop, after the
other experiments, each as a single, mostly autonomous session that used open-source tools only. We set
the goal and stopped the session, but we suggested no method and wrote no code. Section 7 compares the
modes.
5.4
Verification
We have not relied on the checkers written by the agents. For each problem family, a separate checker,
which shares no code with the solvers, verifies every schedule. The FJSPT checker uses exact fractions,
because some layouts use half time units. We have also tested the checkers on deliberately corrupted
schedules, and they rejected all of them. Each instance file was compared with the original distribution
and with independent copies. A single script in the public repository re-checks every result of this paper.
We take the lower bounds of the libraries and the literature as published, but not the single-solver verdicts
of our baseline runs. An instance is closed only when a certified schedule reaches such a bound or a bound
of Section 3.2 proved by two solvers.
5.5
Contamination controls
The instances are public, and they may be part of the training data of the models. However, no schedule with
the makespans reported here existed before this work, so a new best-known value cannot be reproduced
from memory, and every value is certified by the independent checker. The containers of the autonomous
runs had public network access, but no session used a web search or fetch tool, and no session downloaded
benchmark data, bounds, or published solutions. The autonomous runs received only the instance and the
task text, and for behnke16 a small example instance and schedule. One job-shop session also received
earlier code (Section 5). The target values of the job-shop runs came from the first interactive session
(Section 5.6). The assisted transport-robot session started from one message that pasted the paper of Meng
et al. (2023) and asked the agent to choose the instance with the best chance of improvement and to find
tailored solutions rather than to rely on computation. During the session, we supplied the further papers
that it requested, including published schedules. It used these schedules only to validate its model and data
(Section 6.1). No commercial solver was available to any agent.
5.6
Reporting and repetitions
Table 3 lists every autonomous run and every interactive agent session on the instances of this paper, as
they were recorded, including the runs that missed the target, failed, or stopped early. No run has been
removed on the basis of its result. Runs on other problems, and on instances that we generated to calibrate
the tasks, are not included. The instance tai_100_1000_1 was chosen in the first interactive session, after
a greedy pilot run, and the target values of the autonomous job-shop runs came from that session. For the
assisted Behnke session, no transcript was kept. The transport-robot study was one long assisted session
in which the agent made 380 solver runs. For it, we report the best schedules, a fixed protocol of 100 runs
(Table 8), and the controlled comparisons of moves (Sections 6.1 and 6.4).
Because the provider does not expose sampling seeds, we measure the run-to-run variation of the
agents by repeated sessions with the same task. On tai_100_1000_1, the six Claude Opus 5 sessions,
one of which received earlier code (Section 5), ended between 527,000 and 533,386 (median 531,403),
and the nine Claude Sonnet 5 sessions that delivered a schedule between 535,930 and 554,332 (median
541,641). On behnke16, the twelve autonomous sessions ended between 404 and 479 (median 418). The
solvers written by the agents are re-run with explicit seeds, and we report the best value together with the
range or the median of the runs (Tables 5 and 8).

6.1
How the agents found their solutions
The agents have not applied one fixed algorithm. In the successful runs, the agent first analyzed the instance
and then adapted the formulation or the method to its structure. This subsection describes the main ideas,
and Sections 6.2–6.6 report the results.
6.1.1
Change of formulation for the job shop
In tai_100_1000_1, each job visits 1,000 machines. The machines are idle about 90% of the time, while
each job is busy for about 91–99% of the time. The longest job alone needs 522,298 time units, which
is the lower bound. The best of the autonomous sessions (Figure 2) started from a greedy schedule of
593,321 and wrote four solvers that minimized the makespan, and the best of them reached 592,865. At
minute 42, the agent changed the formulation. It fixed a target makespan T and searched for a schedule
with no machine conflict and Cmax ≤T. To this end, the agent restricted each operation of job j to a
corridor
prefj(o) ≤sj,o ≤prefj(o) + (T −Lj),
where Lj is the length of job j and prefj(o) is the start of operation o when the job runs without idle
time. Inside these corridors, Cmax ≤T always holds. The corridors alone do not ensure the job order,
because two consecutive operations of a job may overlap while each of them lies inside its own corridor.
The search therefore starts from the schedule sj,o = prefj(o) + (T −Lj) o/m, in which the delay of an
operation does not decrease along its job, and it maintains the job order at every iteration. When it shifts
an operation, it also shifts the successors or the predecessors of this operation on the job as far as required,
and it rejects the shift if an operation would leave its corridor or if more than 60 operations would move.
Thus, only machine conflicts remain. A min-conflicts search with random perturbations removes them,
8


--- Page 9 ---
and each time it finds a feasible schedule, the agent lowers T. At each iteration, the search selects two
overlapping operations on a machine, evaluates the four shifts that separate them, and applies the shift
that yields the smallest total overlap, or a random feasible shift with a probability of 8%. After 200,000
iterations without improvement, it shifts random operations of machines with overlaps. After a feasible
schedule, T decreases by 1,000, and after 40 million iterations without improvement, the search restarts
from the best schedule with a random target below its makespan. The first corridor prototype, started at
T = 545,000, found a schedule of 540,999 after about 60 s, at minute 46 of the session. The agent then
wrote a faster C version (csp3.c) and ran 28 worker processes (16 of csp3 and 12 of a variant) on the
4 CPUs of the container. A csp3 worker found 527,000 at about minute 77, and the agent saved it at
minute 81 of a session that lasted 101.6 minutes. Figure 3a shows this session.

6.1.2
Stage structure of the flexible job shop
The best session on behnke16 analyzed the eligibility sets and found that the instance is a three-stage
flexible flow shop: operation 0 of each job runs on machines 1–4, operations 1–3 on machines 5–16,
and operation 4 on machines 17–20. The last stage is the bottleneck. The agent then wrote a parallel
tabu search with ruin-and-recreate moves. After each move, a fast procedure re-optimizes the machine
assignment of the first and the last stage. With the rest of the schedule fixed, each of these stages reduces
to a partition problem. A secondary criterion counts the operations near the critical path and breaks ties
among schedules of equal makespan. The session improved a constructive solution of 448 down to 404. It
9


--- Page 10 ---
ran about 31 worker threads in a container with a quota of 4 CPUs. The other four sessions of this batch
used tabu search, simulated annealing, CP-SAT, and large neighborhood search, and ended between 411
and 419. One session used CP-SAT with a warm start and proved that 226 is optimal for behnke31.
6.1.3
Routing structure of the problem with transport robots
In the assisted FJSPT session, we gave the agent the benchmark, one recent paper with published results
(Meng et al., 2023), and the goal of improving the best-known values. We also asked it to exploit the
structure of the problem rather than rely on more computation, and during the session we supplied the
recent papers that it requested. The agent then executed the following steps:
1. It used MKT10, the largest MKT instance, as the main development instance.
2. It replayed the published schedules of two competing papers (Meng et al., 2023; Berterottière et al.,
2024) with an independent checker. All of them reproduced the published makespans exactly, which
confirmed that the model and the data match the literature.
3. It analyzed good schedules and found that both vehicles are almost never idle and that most arcs
of the critical path connect consecutive tasks of the same vehicle. In other words, the problem is
mainly a two-vehicle pickup-and-delivery routing problem.
4. It wrote a simulated annealing solver with moves borrowed from vehicle routing: relocation, ex-
change, 2-opt∗(Potvin and Rousseau, 1995), and ruin-and-recreate (Schrimpf et al., 2000).
5. It ran controlled experiments, kept the moves that improved the results, and removed the others.
6.2
Job shop
Autonomous sessions (mode A)
Sixteen autonomous sessions worked on tai_100_1000_1: six with
Claude Opus 5 and ten with Claude Sonnet 5. Fifteen of them delivered a feasible schedule, and one
stopped after 18 minutes without a schedule. Figure 2 shows the final makespan of each session, numbered
in order of makespan. The horizontal lines show the job-chain lower bound (ScheduleOpt, 2026b), the best
value of this work, the tracked OptalCP bound (ScheduleOpt, 2026b,c), and the Hexaly bound (Yuraszeck
et al., 2026). Five of the six Opus sessions finished below the tracked OptalCP bound of 533,080. All six
Opus sessions ended below the nine Sonnet sessions that delivered a schedule (at most 533,386 against
at least 535,930). All 15 schedules are below the 10-minute CP-SAT value (554,381), and 13 are below
the 10-minute CP Optimizer value (545,805). The best session reached 527,000 with 4 CPUs, in 101.6
minutes and with an API cost of US$10.07.
Agent solver (mode B)
The best session left its solver, csp3.c, in the container. We have recovered
the source from the session log and have run it with one core per worker. Twelve workers ran for 1,800 s
each. All twelve finished below the 527,000 of the session, and five below 526,000. The best worker (F14
in Figure 3b) reached 525,764 after 23 minutes. Six workers started with the target 531,000 and six with
527,000, the result of the session. The best worker was one of the first six. The logs do not record the host,
but the iteration rates match one core per worker. Within the session, the solver did not reach 526,000.
This is due to the fact that its 28 processes shared 4 CPUs, which reduced the iteration rate of each process
to about one tenth of that of a process with its own core. On a single core, the same solver reaches 533,000,
the tracked OptalCP value, in 2.7–5.1 s when it starts with this target, and in 7.8–16.2 s when it starts at
535,000. With the 16-core budget of our CP Optimizer runs (16 workers with their own cores and different
seeds for 1,800 s, three such runs), the same solver reached 525,515, the best value of this work.

Comparison with solvers
Table 4 compares these results with the published values of commercial and
open-source solvers. The gap is relative to the lower bound of 522,298. The JSPLib values come from
a standard 10-minute run on a 4-core laptop processor (Intel Core i7-1185G7). JSPLib does not state
the number of threads. The tracked OptalCP value comes from a run of 180 minutes. JSPLib lists the
processor of our workstation (Ryzen 9 5950X) for this run, but the published run record of OptalCP gives
version 2026.2, 16 workers, and an AMD EPYC 9454P (OptalCP, 2026a). The hardware, versions, and
thread counts of the other published rows are those stated by the sources. Da Col and Teppan (2022) used
CP Optimizer 12.10 on an AMD EPYC 7551P, and Yuraszeck et al. (2026) used Hexaly 14.0 on an Intel
Core i7-10750H with all 12 threads. Because these published values come from different hardware and
budgets, we have also run CP Optimizer 22.2 and Hexaly 15.0 ourselves on our workstation, with the same
budgets as the agent solver (Tables 4, 5, and 10). These rows are labeled “ours”. The 1-core and 16-core
rows of our runs are the best of three runs, and a 16-core run of the agent solver consists of 16 single-core
workers with different seeds. For both, we have used the standard job-shop model of the vendor with
default parameters. Hexaly reached 541,764 with one core and 539,566 with 16 cores after 30 minutes,
better than its published value of 542,479 and than CP Optimizer, but 2.7% above the agent solver with 16
cores. Our Hexaly license allowed one process at a time, so each Hexaly run had the workstation to itself.

Generalization to similar instances
tai_100_1000_1 belongs to a family of ten instances of the same
size and type, all of them open in JSPLib. We have run the corridor solver just described on all ten without
any change, with three runs per instance with different seeds, one core, and 1,800 s per run. Table 5 shows
11


--- Page 12 ---
the results. In Table 5, LB is the length of the longest job, “Best known” the JSPLib upper bound before
this work, and “OptalCP 10 min” the standard JSPLib run (ScheduleOpt, 2026b). CP Optimizer 22.2 and
block 1 of the agent solver are the best of three seeds with one core after 10 and 30 minutes. The agent
solver starts at T = ⌈1.02 LB/1000⌉· 1000. Block 2 and the 16-core runs are described below. In the
column “Best”, bold values are below the best-known value.
The solver found a schedule below the best-known upper bound on every instance, already after 10
minutes, far below the 10-minute values of OptalCP, CP Optimizer, and CP-SAT. With one core and 30
minutes, CP Optimizer 22.2 ended 3.7–5.8% and Hexaly 15.0 2.7–4.4% above the lower bound, and with
16 cores 2.6–5.3% and 2.4–4.2%. Both stayed above the old best-known value on every instance, whereas
the agent solver ended 0.0–1.8% and 0.0–1.6% above the lower bound. Over the three runs and the ten
instances, the mean gap with one core is 0.73% for the agent solver, 4.49% for CP Optimizer, and 3.60%
for Hexaly, and with 16 cores 0.53%, 3.79%, and 3.30%. At both budgets, the worst run of the agent
solver is below the best run of both commercial solvers on all ten instances. On tai_100_1000_2 and
_3, the solver found a makespan equal to the lower bound, so these two instances are now closed. Two of
the three seeds found each optimum, that of _3 in less than 10 minutes. A second block of sixteen further
runs of 1,800 s with two processes per core improved five instances further but closed none, because each
process had only half a core. Finally, with the 16-core budget of CP Optimizer (three runs of 16 single-core
workers with different seeds), the solver found the optima of _2 and _3 in all runs and improved seven
instances further. On _7, all three runs ended at 527,000.
Improvement campaign (mode C)
Starting from the corridor solver and the schedules above, one
Claude Opus 5.5 session worked for 24 h on a 4-core ARM cloud machine (about 84 core-hours of solver
runs), with the goal of closing the ten instances. It made three changes to the solver. First, it started the
search directly at the lower bound instead of descending in steps of 1,000. Second, it narrowed the time
window of every operation by constraint propagation at that target. Third, it reduced the size of the random
perturbations of the local search. With these changes, it found schedules whose makespan equals the lower
bound on _4 (527,101) and _9 (528,097), so four of the ten instances are now closed, and it improved _8
to 527,280. Among the 191 logged runs of this campaign, one of the 34 runs with the target at the lower
bound succeeded on _4, one of 34 on _9, none of 58 on _8, and none of 23 on _6. It also found that our
schedules contain small idle gaps, and starting every operation as early as possible while keeping the order
on each machine has lowered the other five values by 126–229 units. The session re-found the optimum of
_2 in 47 s on one core. Table 14 in Appendix A lists all values.
6.3
Flexible job shop
Table 6 lists all runs on the three Behnke instances (bold: below the best-known upper bound of FJSPLib).
Of ten autonomous sessions on behnke16 with a target of 411, the best reached 404 and a second one 411,
both below the best-known 412. Three sessions stopped by themselves after 4–7% of the budget, and one
after 462 s because of an API error. Of two further sessions on all three instances, one found and proved
the optimum of 226 on behnke31. In an assisted session, the agent wrote a reusable tabu search, which
found 406 on behnke16 in 56.5 s with 32 threads and the optimum on behnke31, but did not improve
behnke14 (232 against 230).

Generalization to the full Behnke set
Behnke and Geiger (2012) published 60 instances, of which
FJSPLib lists 32 as open and 28 as closed at the commit that we have used (f89e5b0, checked on October
11, 2026). We have run the reusable tabu search of the agent on all 60 without any change. As baselines,
we have also run standard models in CP-SAT and in CP Optimizer 22.2 with the same budget, with one run
of 120 s with 8 threads per instance and method, on the same workstation. Both models use one optional
interval for each eligible machine of an operation, which is the usual model for the flexible job shop. The
tabu search and CP-SAT runs ran three at a time on the 16 cores, and the CP Optimizer runs two at a time,
so CP Optimizer had slightly more cores per run. In a second block, we have given the tabu search one
run of 1,200 s with 16 threads on each open instance. These runs ran two at a time, so each had about 8
cores, half the cores of the original behnke16 run (32 threads on the 16 cores). CP Optimizer received
the same 1,200 s with 16 threads, but one run at a time, so it had twice the cores of the tabu search in this
block. Hexaly 15.0 ran with its standard flexible job-shop model, the same time limits and threads, and
one run at a time. An independent checker verified all 336 schedules. Each value comes from a single run
per instance and method. Differences of one or two units on a single instance are within the run-to-run
variation (the 1,200 s run of the tabu search ended worse than its 120 s run on behnke55 and behnke59).
Table 7 shows the results, and the public repository contains the values of all 60 instances. The table lists
the open instances on which the tabu search or CP-SAT has reached or improved the best-known upper
bound of FJSPLib (ScheduleOpt, 2026a). With 1,200 s, CP Optimizer also reached it on behnke15 and
behnke52. TTB is the time in seconds to the best value of the 1,200 s run of the tabu search, bold values
are below the best-known value, and the superscript o marks a value that CP-SAT has reported as optimal.

With 120 s, the tabu search went below the best-known upper bound on 5 of the 32 open instances,
matched it on 2 more, and found the optimum on 18 of the 28 closed instances. On average, it was 0.60%
above the best-known upper bound, against 1.42% for CP Optimizer, 2.85% for Hexaly, and 6.42% for
CP-SAT. It was better than CP Optimizer on 31 instances, equal on 21, and worse on 8. With 1,200 s on
the open instances, the tabu search went below the best-known upper bound on 10 of them and matched it
on 4 more, and it was 0.24% above it on average, against 0.79% for CP Optimizer with all 16 cores and
2.01% for Hexaly. It was better than CP Optimizer on 19 open instances, equal on 9, and worse on 4. CP
Optimizer went below the best-known upper bound on 7 open instances and found a new best-known value
of 221 on behnke34. Hexaly improved no best-known value. A re-run of the tabu search with the same
cores as CP Optimizer gave 0.45% and 0.34%. Over both blocks, the tabu search improved the best-known
upper bound of 11 of the 32 open instances. CP-SAT found the optimum on 19 closed instances and
reported 212 on behnke53 and 125 on behnke48 as optimal. Following the rule of Section 5.4, we do not
count these verdicts. However, FJSPLib now lists behnke48 as closed and behnke53 with a lower bound
of 212, so our CP-SAT schedule of 212 closes behnke53 with respect to the current library. On the large
13


--- Page 14 ---
instances, CP-SAT was often 10–23% above the best-known value.
Improvement campaign (mode C)
Starting from the two Behnke solvers of the agents and the schedules
above, one Claude Fable 5.1 session worked for 13.5 h on our workstation, with open-source tools only
and the goal of closing as many instances as possible. It merged the two solvers into a new local search
and used CP-SAT to search for schedules with a given makespan. The campaign reached the FJSPLib
lower bound on six open instances (behnke32, 34, 40, 55, 56, and 60), which are therefore closed, and on
all 28 closed instances. Thus, 34 of the 60 instances now have a schedule at the lower bound. Its values
are below the best-known upper bound on 18 of the 32 open instances, against 11 for modes A and B.
The new local search produced most of the improvements on the 100-job instances, and eight of the new
values, including the six closures, came from CP-SAT runs that the agent started with a fixed or capped
makespan (Table 14). Other processes ran on the workstation at the same time, so we do not compare run
times. FJSPLib has changed during this study. Its current version (commit 8a6e36e, 22 October 2026)
lists 27 open instances. Another contributor reported the same values as this campaign for behnke52 and
behnke60 on 12 October, one week before the campaign, and CP-SAT runs raised several lower bounds.
With respect to this version, the values of this campaign remain below the upper bound on 16 instances
and close six (behnke32, 34, 38, 40, 55, and 56). On 9 November 2026, a further report to FJSPLib has
claimed values equal to ours on behnke32, 34, 40, and 55 and better on behnke35, 53, 57, and 59 (on
behnke53, equal to our CP-SAT value of 212), whereas our 387 on behnke38 is better than its 388.
6.4
Flexible job shop with transport robots
Lower bounds
We have re-implemented the bounds of Section 3.2 independently. CP-SAT and CPLEX
proved the same optimal values of bound (1) on all 51 instances, and CP-SAT and CP Optimizer those of
relaxation (3) on all Chambers–Barnes, small, and medium instances, before any rounding. No bound is
above any of the 177 schedules certified by our checker, the 40 replayed schedules of Han et al. (2024)
and Meng et al. (2025), or the 18 proven optima, and no bound exceeds the optimum of 403 random and
sub-sampled instances. The bounds of Homayouni and Fontes (2021), recomputed on our files, reproduce
their published values except on MKT03 and MKT04, which suggests that their experiments on these
two instances used other data. An earlier relaxation written by an agent in this study is a special case of
bound (1). Details are in the public repository.
Structure of the solutions
In the best MKT10 schedule, with a makespan of 499, the two vehicles are
never idle. They carry jobs for 809 time units and drive empty for 172.5 units, so the makespan is half of
this work plus a tail of about 8 units. On the critical path, 64 of 71 arcs connect consecutive tasks of the
same vehicle when ties are broken toward job arcs (Figure 4). The left panel of this figure shows the two
vehicles (dark for loaded travel, light for empty travel) and the machines over time. The right panel shows
the share of vehicle, job, and machine arcs on the critical path of the best schedules of MKT04, MKT06,
and MKT10.
Progress over time
During the assisted session, the first runs on MKT10, 20 minutes into the session,
found 541.5, already below all values published before 2025. The 2-opt∗route exchange gave the largest
gain of any single move (548 to 537.5 at equal budget). Slower cooling then yielded 522, ruin-and-recreate
518, and long independent runs 499 after 2.9 hours. The run that found 499 used one thread for 31 minutes.
By then, the campaign had used about 40 thread-hours on MKT10.

All reproduce their makespans and are feasible, except on MKT05, where the schedules of 290 (Han et al.,
2024) and 286 (Meng et al., 2025) assign an operation to a machine on which it is not eligible in the

two schedules were accepted, MKT05 would be a tie, and six of the ten instances would be improved.

it is 293 and not shown. “Change” is relative to it, and “Below” counts the runs of the protocol (ten
independent 20-minute single-thread runs per instance, 28 concurrent processes on 32 threads) that are
below it. The last column is one 10-minute CP-SAT run with 8 threads from a greedy start. The lower
bounds that CP-SAT proved in these runs (61 to 587) are below LB on all ten instances.
On seven of the ten instances (MKT01, MKT03, MKT05, MKT06, MKT08, MKT09, and MKT10),
the certified makespans are below the reference value. The largest changes are −6.1% on MKT03, −5.4%
on MKT09, and −5.0% on MKT10. On all ten instances, the agent solver is at least as good as the CP
Optimizer models of Meng et al. (2025), which ran for 3,600 s, and it is better on nine. The CP-assisted
genetic algorithm of the same study reports 237 on MKT04, one unit below our 238, without a published
schedule for this instance. The HA-DQN values on MKT01, MKT04, and MKT05 (153, 213, and 251)
15


--- Page 16 ---
and the LAHC value on MKT04 (225) are below LB, and the closed-form bound of Section 3.2 (165, 234,
and 282) is sufficient to show this. If one counts all published values without these checks, our values
are below all of them on five instances. On MKT02 and MKT07, Dong et al. (2025) report 122 and 243,
below our 124 and 245. These two values are not below LB, and they were published without schedules,
so we could not check them. With respect to LB, our best schedules are 0.4–14.3% above it. On MKT05,
the schedule of 286 is only one unit above the bound of 285. As a fixed protocol, we have run the final
solver ten times for 20 minutes on each instance (Table 8). On the seven instances just mentioned, 61 of
the 70 runs are below the reference value.
Chambers–Barnes instances
Table 9 gives the results on the 21 Chambers–Barnes transport instances.
In this table, LB is relaxation (3) of Section 3.2, which CP-SAT and CP Optimizer solve to optimality on
all 21 instances. “L/I/D” is the smallest value of LAHC (Homayouni and Fontes, 2021), IGA (Meng et al.,
2023), and DCGA (Han et al., 2024), “DRL” the value of HA-DQN (Dong et al., 2025), and “CP” the best
value of Meng et al. (2025). A dagger marks a CP value without a published schedule. All other CP values
are the makespans of the published schedules replayed with our checker, which differ from the reported
values on mt10xyzt (901 instead of 916), seti5xxxt (1,316 instead of 1,318), and seti5cct, whose
schedule omits a transport of zero length and needs 1,263 instead of 1,261 when it is inserted. The column
∆is relative to the smallest published value that is not below LB. The agent-written solver is better than
L/I/D on 12 of the 21 instances. However, the approach of Meng et al. (2025), based on CP Optimizer,
is better than our solver on 20 instances and equal on mt10xyt, where both schedules are optimal. Our
solver is 0.0–6.5% above the best published value. It is weaker on these instances because processing
times are much longer than travel times, and the critical path consists of machine arcs only, which a routing
neighborhood cannot shorten. The relaxation remains informative. Seven HA-DQN values, published
without schedules, are below LB, among them 872 and 816 on mt10xxxt and mt10xyzt, which are also
below the optima of the same instances without transport in FJSPLib (ScheduleOpt, 2026a). Meng et al.
(2025) report 14 of the 21 instances as proven optimal. On seven of them, their published schedule reaches
LB (asterisks in Table 9), which confirms optimality independently of their solver. On mt10xyzt, under
the benchmark model, which the schedules of Meng et al. (2023) and Berterottière et al. (2024) reproduce
exactly, their schedule has a makespan of 901, equal to LB. The reported 916 may come from a different
evaluation.

Generalization to other FJSPT instances
We have run the final transport solver without any change on
the other two-vehicle sets of Homayouni and Fontes (2021): ten small instances (SFJST) and ten medium
instances (MFJST, built from the instances of Fattahi et al. 2007). Before the runs, we have checked the
instance files, and the published schedules of Berterottière et al. (2024) and Meng et al. (2023) replay to
their published makespans on these files. Each instance received five runs of 60 s on one thread. On the
small instances, 48 of the 50 runs found the proven optimum, and every instance was solved to optimality
by at least four runs. The medium instances are less uniform. The solver found the proven optimum
(Homayouni and Fontes, 2021) on MFJST01, 03, and 06 in at least one of five runs, and matched the best
16


--- Page 17 ---
published value of 900 on MFJST08, which equals relaxation (3) and is therefore optimal. On MFJST02,
04, 05, and 07, its best run stayed 0.5–2.3% above the optimal value. On MFJST09, it found 1,090, below
the values of DCGA and IVNDGA (Han et al., 2024; Jia et al., 2025) but above the 1,075 of Meng et al.
(2025), whose schedule we replayed and which equals relaxation (3), so it is optimal. On MFJST10, it
stayed 1.4% above the best published value of 1,227. These instances have long processing times compared
with the travel times, and the final temperatures of the annealing (0.2 to 4 time units) are too small for
them. We have not tuned the solver for these instances, because the goal was to test the unchanged method.
Open-source baseline
As an open-source baseline, we have run CP-SAT on a complete constraint model
of the problem. The model uses optional intervals for the machine choice and a multiple-circuit constraint
for the routes of the two vehicles, with empty travel times that depend on the chosen machines. It accepts
every published schedule and every schedule of this work as feasible. CP-SAT started from a greedy
dispatch schedule and ran for 10 minutes with 8 threads on the same workstation. Table 8 compares its
result with the ten 20-minute single-thread runs of the agent solver. Although the agent solver used a
quarter of the CPU time (1,200 thread-seconds against 4,800), CP-SAT ended 6–112% above the median
of the agent solver.

7
Discussion
7.1
The agent as the solver, as the author of a solver, or as its improver
Table 12 compares modes A and B of Section 5.3.
In mode A, the agent itself is the algorithm. The user needs neither optimization knowledge nor code,
and the agent adapts to each instance, up to changing the formulation. The job-shop session moved to a
fixed-target formulation with time windows, a known technique in exact job-shop methods (Carlier and
Pinson, 1994), and applied it at a scale of 100,000 operations. However, every new schedule requires a
new session, which on tai_100_1000_1 cost US$2.43–22.69 and took 18–300 minutes, and the results
vary considerably (527,000 to 554,332).
Table 12. Modes A and B of a coding agent
Mode A: the agent is the solver
Mode B: the agent writes a solver
Output
one schedule
a reusable program
Development cost (once)
none
one session: US$10 (autonomous,
101.6 min) or an assisted session (5–12 h)
Cost of a new schedule
a new session: US$2–23
CPU time only
Time to a new schedule
0.3–5 h
seconds to 30 minutes
Run-to-run variance
high
low; controlled by seeds
Repeatable
no
yes
Similar instances
new session each
runs unchanged
New structure
adapts by itself
needs a new session
Auditable
partly (transcript)
fully (source code)
In mode B, the agent writes a solver once, and from then on a new schedule costs only CPU time.
Because the solver is code, an expert can read it, test it, and change it. It is also repeatable. We have
recompiled the transport solver from its source, have used the same seed, and have obtained a schedule
identical to the MKT10 schedule of this paper. The solvers also apply to similar instances without change
(Section 6). On the job-shop family, the solver from one session has improved all ten instances and has
closed two of them. The reusable tabu search has improved the best-known upper bound of 11 open
Behnke instances, and the transport solver has found every optimum on the small transport instances. The
18


--- Page 19 ---
drawback is that a solver tailored to one structure can be weak on another. The transport solver is strong
when the vehicles are the bottleneck and weaker when the machines are (Section 6.4).
In practice, the two modes work best together. An agent session identifies the structure of a problem
and produces a method. A short assisted session then turns this method into a solver that the user runs again
whenever a new instance with a similar structure arrives. This matches a common situation in industry,
where a plant solves the same type of problem every day with different data.
Mode C follows from these results. Once the solvers of mode B had been applied to whole instance
families without change, we studied whether an agent can take the next step without human input: start
from everything that modes A and B produced and coordinate its own campaign. In both campaigns, the
agent planned the experiments, changed or combined the solvers, distributed the runs over the cores, and
abandoned some search directions. We only set the goal and stopped the session. On the job shop, it
analyzed why the corridor solver stalls close to the lower bound and changed the search instead of adding
compute. On the Behnke instances, it merged the two agent-written solvers and used CP-SAT at a fixed
makespan. The three modes thus form a sequence: an agent produces a method, the method becomes a
reusable solver, and an agent then improves this solver with the results obtained so far. A campaign needs
more time and compute than a single run (24 and 13.5 hours), but still no expert work and no commercial
software.
7.2
Quality, speed, and cost
In terms of quality, Section 6.5 gives the numbers. The published values of the commercial solvers come
from other hardware and from time limits between 10 minutes and 6 hours. Our own runs of CP Optimizer
and Hexaly remove this difference. With the same budget on the same workstation, both were weaker than
the agent solvers on the job shop (2.4–5.3% against 0.0–1.6% above the lower bound with 16 cores), and
weaker on the Behnke instances, where CP Optimizer nevertheless found the new best-known value 221 on
behnke34. On the transport instances, the agent solver beats a published approach based on CP Optimizer
when the vehicles are the bottleneck (MKT), but not when the machines are (Chambers–Barnes). Some
agent results used more total CPU time than the reference runs, and the solver budgets do not include the
time needed to develop the agent solvers (see below).
In terms of speed, the agent-written solvers are also fast. On one core, the corridor solver reaches the
180-minute OptalCP value of tai_100_1000_1 in 2.7–16.2 s, the reusable tabu found 406 on behnke16
after 56.5 s, and the first runs of the transport session were below all MKT10 values published before 2025
after 20 minutes. Developing a solver takes longer: 101.6 minutes for the corridor solver, and about 5 and
12 hours for the two recorded assisted sessions.
In terms of cost, we separate the cost of developing a solver from the cost of a new schedule. The
16 autonomous job-shop sessions took 48 hours in total and cost US$167 in API charges for the 15 with
a recorded cost (median US$12.72). The session that wrote the corridor solver cost US$10.07. The
interactive sessions ran under a Claude Max subscription (US$100 per month) on a few days, together less
than one month of subscription time, so we estimate their cost at about US$100. The two campaigns of
mode C also ran within such a plan. At API list prices, the logged token use of the two recorded interactive
sessions would cost about US$199. Our own time for goals, review, and verification is not included. Once
a solver exists, each new schedule costs only CPU time on commodity hardware and needs no license,
whereas a developer subscription of CP Optimizer starts at US$320 per user and month (IBM, 2026). A
general-purpose solver must work well on every instance, whereas the agent can specialize to one structure.
This specialization appears to be the main source of its advantage.
7.3
Limitations
We have tested only models from one provider (Anthropic), namely Claude Opus and Claude Sonnet, and
Claude Fable in one campaign of mode C. Controlled comparisons across models and problem classes are
needed to show which models are suitable for this task (Section 8).
All instances are benchmarks from the literature. Their generators can give them regular structure, for
19


--- Page 20 ---
example the long, almost idle machines of the 100 × 1000 job shops or the clear stages of behnke16, and
the agents have exploited such structure. It should be noted, however, that our conclusions may not hold
for industrial problems, which are often less regular and include additional constraints.
The agents did not raise the lower bound of any job-shop or Behnke instance.
On the transport
instances, the agent of the assisted session wrote a relaxation that bound (1) of Section 3.2 generalizes.
The closed instances (tai_100_1000_2, _3, _4, and _9, and six Behnke instances in mode C) are closed
because the schedules reach the known lower bound. tai_100_1000_1 and behnke16 remain open.
The generalization runs used short budgets and few seeds (three runs of 30 minutes, or single runs of
120 s and 1,200 s). We ran CP Optimizer and Hexaly with standard models and default parameters, as a
typical user would. Models or parameters tuned by an expert for these instances may yield better results.
On the medium transport instances, the unchanged solver stayed above the best known value on six of ten
instances.
MKT10 served as the main development instance of the transport solver, which may favor it. For this
reason, we report the full instance sets. On the Chambers–Barnes instances, whose critical paths consist
of machine arcs, the transport solver is weaker than a recent approach based on CP Optimizer (Meng
et al., 2025). A solver tailored to the vehicles does not transfer to instances in which the machines are the
bottleneck. Finally, Dong et al. (2025) report lower values than ours on five MKT instances. Three of
these values are below our lower bound. They do not publish schedules, so we could not check the other
two with our checker.
8
Conclusions and future research
We have examined whether a frontier LLM coding agent can replace a commercial solver on difficult
scheduling problems. On three established problem families, the agents found schedules better than the
best published values, using only open-source tools and their own code. In autonomous sessions, without
expert knowledge, they improved the 100,000-operation job shop tai_100_1000_1 and the flexible job
shop behnke16. The solvers they wrote transfer to similar instances: unchanged, the job-shop solver
improved all ten instances of its family and closed two, and in mode C agents closed two further job shops
and six flexible job shops. With transport robots, the agent solver improved seven of the ten MKT instances
but none of the Chambers–Barnes instances, on which a CP Optimizer approach is better. New, validated
lower bounds for this problem are above eleven published values on the distributed instance files and certify
eight published schedules as optimal. On large benchmark instances with exploitable structure, solvers
written by current LLM agents can match or beat commercial solvers, both their published values and our
own runs of CP Optimizer and Hexaly with the same budget. The cost is low. The job-shop solver took
one autonomous session of 101.6 minutes and US$10, and each new schedule then costs only CPU time.
The agents are strongest when an instance has a structure that a general-purpose solver does not exploit.
This study provides evidence for models from one provider, three model lines, and three problem
families, which were selected because they are open, large, and structurally rich. It does not show how
other models perform, or how the results transfer to other classes of optimization problems. More studies
are therefore required that compare different models on a wide range of optimization problems under
controlled conditions. Such studies should vary the model family and size, keep the task text, the tools,
the compute resources, and the time budget fixed, and report all runs, so that differences in performance
can be attributed to the models.
A natural next step is a standardized benchmark for this purpose. It would collect established instances
from many problem classes, for example the job shop, the flexible job shop, the open shop (Gonzalez and
Sahni, 1976), scheduling with transport resources, nurse rostering (Ceschia et al., 2018), and timetabling
(McCollum et al., 2010), each with its source, its best-known bounds, and an independent checker. Runs
of several model families on the same benchmark would show how each model performs on each problem
class, and the evaluation of new model versions on the same tasks would show how this performance
changes over time. A benchmark that covers many problem classes would also reduce the risk of an
instance selection that favors one method, which is a limitation of the present study.
20


--- Page 21 ---
A second open question is which behavior of the agents yields good solutions. Here, a change of
formulation and the use of instance structure were decisive, but on a small number of sessions.
A
systematic analysis of many sessions could test whether these strategies are general.
Data and materials availability
All materials of this study are available in a public repository at https://github.com/andrealbrechtl/
agent-heuristics-jobshop-supplement/. For each problem family, it contains the instance files with their
sources and checksums, the certified schedules, an independent checker, the solver source code, the run
commands, and the solver logs. It also contains the replays of published schedules (Meng et al., 2023;
Berterottière et al., 2024; Han et al., 2024; Meng et al., 2025), the models, schedules, and logs of our CP
Optimizer, Hexaly, and CP-SAT baselines, the campaigns of mode C, and the scripts and results of the
lower bounds of Section 3.2. For setb4xxx, the distributed data file repeats the block of seti5xxx, and
we used the original Chambers–Barnes data. The task texts of the autonomous job-shop and behnke16
runs and the first message of the assisted transport-robot session are included verbatim. The other runs
used the same or very similar task texts. One script re-checks every value in this paper.
Use of generative AI
The use of LLM coding agents to produce the experimental results is the subject of the study and is
described in Section 5. During the preparation of the manuscript, the authors used Claude (Anthropic) to
review the text and to rewrite parts of it. The lower bounds of Section 3.2 were derived and implemented
by Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5, in Claude Code, November 2026) during the review of the
manuscript. Bound (1) generalizes a relaxation written earlier by the agent of the transport session. The
authors re-implemented and validated them independently with two solvers. The authors have checked the
proofs. The authors reviewed and edited all content and take full responsibility for the publication.

New best-known values found by the agents
Table 13 lists every instance on which an agent of mode A or B found a new best-known value (Section 6.6),
and Table 14 the values of mode C below both the best value of modes A and B (A/B) and the previous
best-known value. LB and UB are the best-known bounds before this work (JSPLib, FJSPLib, and, for
MKT, the bound of Homayouni and Fontes (2021) and the reference value of Table 8). “Run” gives the
resources of the run that found the value (16 × 1 core: 16 single-core workers), and “Time” the wall time
to the value (FJSPT: to the end of its cooling run). Notes: a from file timestamps; c one run of a campaign
of about 40 thread-hours; d our CP-SAT baseline later found 212 and reported it as optimal. “Compaction”
starts every operation of the mode-B schedule as early as possible in its machine order, “corridor search”
is the solver of Section 6.2, and “new local search” that of the Behnke campaign.
